Earlier this year, after rolling out managed accounts for children under 13, WhatsApp today expanded its parental supervision features to teenage accounts, adding group activity notifications and additional restrictions on Meta AI. Here's the full story.

WhatsApp expands parental supervision options

Earlier this year, WhatsApp announced a series of new features aimed at giving parents greater control over their children's accounts (under 13).

These include allowing parents to decide who can contact the account, which groups it can join, viewing message requests from unknown contacts, and managing its privacy settings — all changes protected by a parent-set passcode.

A few weeks ago, WhatsApp further expanded this feature on iOS by adding a dedicated "Parental Supervision" section in the Settings app, making it easier for parents to find and configure managed accounts.

WhatsApp is once again expanding these supervision features today, this time extending parental supervision from children under 13 to teenagers, while giving parents greater visibility into group activity and more say over how their children use Channels, status updates, and especially their interactions with Meta AI.

With the update, parents can now receive notifications when their child joins or leaves a group, as well as when an existing group their child is in sees a "significant increase" in membership. Parents can also choose how their child uses Channels, whose status updates they can see, and who can view their child's own status updates.

As for Meta AI, parents can now choose between the standard experience designed for users aged 13 and up, and a stricter "Limited Content" option, depending on what they feel is more appropriate for their child.

WhatsApp says the "Limited Content" setting will further restrict the topics teenagers can discuss with Meta AI. When enabled, Meta AI features that rely on Private Processing will also become unavailable.

WhatsApp reiterated that these parental supervision features do not give parents access to their children's actual messages or calls, as those remain protected by end-to-end encryption.
